questions.q: On per-abdominal examination of a molar pregnancy, how does the fundal height usually compare with the period of gestation?
opts: Fundal height cannot be assessed in mole
questions.exp: The uterus is usually larger than dates (fundal height > POG), rarely ≤ POG. (Book p442)

questions.q: Fill up: In molar pregnancy, fetal parts are ______ on palpation and fetal heart sounds are ______.
questions.exp: Fetal parts are not palpable and fetal heart sounds are absent in molar pregnancy. (Book p442)

questions.q: What uterine consistency is described in molar pregnancy?
questions.exp: The notes describe a doughy uterine consistency in molar pregnancy. (Book p442)

questions.q: Choose the investigation of choice for molar pregnancy and its characteristic finding.
questions.exp: Ultrasound is the IOC and shows the snowstorm appearance. (Book p442)

questions.q: Which item is NOT part of the pre-treatment evaluation before evacuating a mole?
opts: Blood group and Rh with CBC
questions.exp: Pre-treatment evaluation lists LFT, KFT, β-hCG, chest X-ray, blood group/Rh and CBC – not amylase. (Book p442)

questions.q: What is the treatment sequence of choice for molar pregnancy?
opts: Suction evacuation followed by sharp curettage
questions.exp: Suction evacuation followed by sharp curettage is the treatment of choice. (Book p442)

questions.q: During suction evacuation of a mole, which two complications are flagged as increased risks?
questions.exp: The procedure carries ↑ risk of thyrotoxicosis/thyroid storm and pulmonary embolism. (Book p442)

questions.q: When is oxytocin given during suction evacuation of a molar pregnancy?
questions.exp: Oxytocin is given after starting suction evacuation to limit embolisation risk. (Book p442)

questions.q: Hysterectomy for molar pregnancy is indicated in which patient?
questions.exp: Hysterectomy is indicated at age ≥ 40 years with a completed family. (Book p442)

questions.q: Which marker is the IOC for follow-up after molar evacuation?
questions.exp: Serial β-hCG levels are the IOC for follow-up. (Book p442)

questions.q: Arrange the β-hCG follow-up schedule after suction evacuation: (1) weekly till 3 consecutive normal, (2) baseline before procedure, (3) monthly till 6 months, (4) at 48 hours post-evacuation.
questions.exp: Baseline β-hCG, then 48 hrs after evacuation, weekly till 3 consecutive normal, then monthly till 6 months. (Book p442)

questions.q: For how long is pregnancy contraindicated after evacuation of a molar pregnancy?
questions.exp: Pregnancy is contraindicated for 6 months during β-hCG surveillance. (Book p442)

questions.q: Choose the correct contraceptive advice during molar follow-up.
opts: OCP is the contraceptive of choice; IUCD is contraindicated
IUCD is the contraceptive of choice; OCP is contraindicated
Both OCP and IUCD are contraindicated
No contraception is needed if β-hCG is falling
questions.exp: OCPs are the contraceptive of choice while IUCD insertion is contraindicated. (Book p442)

questions.q: Fill up: After evacuation of a hydatidiform mole, beta-hCG is measured ______ until it is normal for three consecutive readings, and then ______ for the rest of follow-up.
questions.exp: Weekly hCG until three consecutive normal values, then monthly for at least six months, reliably detects progression to neoplasia. (Book p442)

questions.q: Fill up: Partial mole arises from ______, whereas complete mole arises from ______.
opts: 1 ovum with 2 sperms; an empty ovum with zygotic chromosome duplication
1 ovum with 1 sperm; 2 ova each fertilized by 1 sperm
2 ova with 2 sperms; 1 ovum fertilized by a single sperm
1 ovum with 1 sperm, in both partial and complete mole
questions.exp: Partial mole arises from 1 ovum fertilized by 2 sperms, whereas complete mole arises from an empty ovum with duplication of the zygotic chromosomes. (Book p443)

questions.q: Which karyotypes characterise a partial mole?
questions.exp: Partial mole is triploid: 69XXY (most common) or 69XXX. (Book p443)

questions.q: Match: partial mole vs complete mole for sperm number and maternal genes.
opts: Partial – dispermic, maternal genes present; complete – monospermic, maternal genes absent
Partial – monospermic, maternal genes absent; complete – dispermic, present
Both dispermic with maternal genes present
Both monospermic with maternal genes absent
questions.exp: Partial mole is dispermic with maternal genes present; complete mole is monospermic with maternal genes absent. (Book p443)

questions.q: p57 KIP2 staining (a marker of maternal genes) is expected to be:
opts: Positive in partial mole, negative in complete mole
Negative in partial mole, positive in complete mole
questions.exp: Maternal genes are present in partial mole (p57 KIP2 +) and absent in complete mole (−). (Book p443)

questions.q: Compare symptom burden and uterine height in partial vs complete mole.
opts: Partial – less common symptoms, uterus < POG; complete – more common symptoms, uterus > POG
Partial – more common symptoms, uterus > POG; complete – less common, < POG
Both have equal symptoms and uterus > POG
Partial – uterus > POG; complete – uterus < POG
questions.exp: Partial mole: symptoms less common and height < POG; complete mole: symptoms more common and height > POG. (Book p443)

questions.q: Which ultrasound picture belongs to a partial mole?
opts: Cystic spaces in placenta with fetal tissue and ↓ amniotic fluid; sac transverse > AP
Snowstorm appearance with bilateral theca lutein cysts
Absent amniotic fluid with no fetal tissue
questions.exp: Partial mole shows placental cystic spaces, fetal tissue (+), reduced fluid and a transverse > AP sac, resembling missed abortion. (Book p443)

questions.q: A 'snowstorm' uterus with no fetal tissue, absent amniotic fluid and bilateral theca lutein cysts indicates:
questions.exp: Those features define the complete/vesicular mole on USG. (Book p443)

questions.q: On HPE (gold standard), which feature separates partial from complete mole?
opts: Vascular villi with less hydropic change in partial; avascular villi with extensive change in complete
Avascular villi in the partial mole; vascular villi in the complete mole
Villi are absent in both partial and complete molar pregnancies
Fetal tissue is absent in the partial mole but present in the complete mole
questions.exp: On HPE, the gold standard, partial mole shows vascular villi with less hydropic change, while complete mole shows avascular villi with extensive hydropic degeneration. (Book p443)

questions.q: What is the risk of subsequent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia after partial vs complete mole?
questions.exp: Subsequent GTN risk is 1% after partial mole and 15–20% after complete mole. (Book p443)

questions.q: The risk of choriocarcinoma after a complete mole is quoted as:
questions.exp: Choriocarcinoma risk is <1% after partial mole and 4% after complete mole. (Book p443)

questions.q: How long does hCG take to return to normal after partial vs complete mole, and what levels are typical before treatment?
opts: 6 weeks vs 7 weeks; <10^5 IU/L vs ≥10^5 IU/L
7 weeks vs 6 weeks; ≥10^5 IU/L vs <10^5 IU/L
12 weeks in both; levels not useful
questions.exp: hCG normalises by 6 weeks (partial) vs 7 weeks (complete); pre-treatment levels are <10^5 IU/L vs ≥10^5 IU/L. (Book p443)

questions.q: Match the trophoblastic entity with its description — 1) Complete mole 2) Partial mole 3) Invasive mole … A) Triploid, usually 69 XXX or 69 XXY, with focal villous swelling and some fetal tissue B) Androgenetic 46 XX with diffuse villous swelling, trophoblastic hyperplasia and no fetus C) Molar villi that invade the myometrium after evacuation and may perforate the uterus
questions.exp: Complete moles are diploid and androgenetic with no fetus; partial moles are triploid with a fetus; invasive moles penetrate the myometrium. (Book p443)

questions.q: Which antecedent pregnancies can be followed by choriocarcinoma according to the causes table?
opts: Molar, full term, ectopic and abortion
questions.exp: Choriocarcinoma (+) follows molar, full term, ectopic and abortion pregnancies. (Book p444)

questions.q: Invasive mole arises only after which pregnancy?
questions.exp: Invasive mole is (+) only after molar pregnancy and (−) after the others. (Book p444)

questions.q: PSTT is uniquely listed as possible after which antecedent pregnancy but NOT after ectopic or abortion?
opts: A term delivery: it is not listed after an ectopic pregnancy or after an abortion
An ectopic pregnancy, which is the antecedent unique to placental site trophoblastic tumour
An abortion, which is the usual antecedent for placental site trophoblastic tumour
None of these, since placental site trophoblastic tumour has no antecedent pregnancy
questions.exp: Placental site trophoblastic tumour characteristically follows a term pregnancy, with a long latency and only modest hCG secretion. (Book p444)

questions.q: Fill up: After a molar pregnancy the m/c GTN is ______, while after a full term pregnancy the m/c GTN is ______.
questions.exp: Molar pregnancy → m/c GTN invasive mole; full term pregnancy → m/c GTN choriocarcinoma. (Book p444)

questions.q: What is the m/c cause of choriocarcinoma?
questions.exp: Molar pregnancy is the m/c cause of choriocarcinoma. (Book p444)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT among the listed signs/symptoms of GTN after hydatidiform mole?
questions.exp: Listed features are persistent bleeding, persistent theca lutein cyst, subinvolution, shock due to invasive mole and metastasis. (Book p444)

questions.q: A plateau of β-hCG over 4 consecutive weekly values (D1, 7, 14, 21) within ±10% suggests:
questions.exp: A β-hCG plateau for 4 consecutive weeks (±10% of previous value) is suggestive of invasive mole. (Book p444)

questions.q: A rise in β-hCG of ≥10% over previous values across 3 weeks (D1, 7, 14) suggests:
questions.exp: An increase ≥10% over 3 weekly values is suggestive of choriocarcinoma. (Book p444)

questions.q: Under the OLD criteria, persisting β-hCG beyond how long after evacuation labelled the case as GTN?
questions.exp: β-hCG present after 6 months of evacuation was the old criterion. (Book p444)

questions.q: What happens to the theca lutein cysts after suction evacuation of a mole?
questions.exp: Theca lutein cysts regress spontaneously in about 2 months after evacuation. (Book p444)

questions.q: What is the m/c site of GTN metastasis and its FIGO stage?
questions.exp: Lung is the m/c metastatic site and corresponds to FIGO stage 3. (Book p444)

questions.q: Which chest X-ray patterns are listed for lung metastases in GTN?
questions.exp: CXR shows cannon ball appearance (m/c) and snowstorm appearance. (Book p444)

questions.q: The second m/c site of GTN metastasis and its typical presentation are:
opts: The vagina just below the urethra, presenting as suburethral nodules
The liver, presenting months later with obstructive jaundice
The brain, presenting with seizures and focal neurological deficits
The pelvis, presenting with deep pelvic pain and a palpable mass
questions.exp: After the lungs, the vagina is the second commonest site: suburethral nodules that may bleed are the classic presentation. (Book p444)

questions.q: Why is biopsy contraindicated in suspected vaginal metastatic nodules of GTN?
opts: Risk of torrential bleeding from highly vascular deposits
Nodules are too small to sample
questions.exp: Biopsy is c/i on these vascular nodules; the notes simply mark it contraindicated. (Book p444)

questions.q: All of the following are characteristic sites of metastasis in gestational trophoblastic neoplasia EXCEPT:
questions.exp: GTN spreads haematogenously to lung, vagina, pelvis, liver and brain; bony metastases are rare and suggest another diagnosis. (Book p444)

questions.q: Match FIGO stage to site in gestational trophoblastic neoplasia: stage 2 and stage 4 correspond to:
opts: Stage 2: disease in the pelvis and vagina — stage 4: brain or liver metastasis
Stage 2: disease confined to the uterine corpus — stage 4: pulmonary metastasis
Stage 2: pulmonary metastasis — stage 4: pelvic and vaginal disease
Stage 2: cerebral metastasis — stage 4: disease still confined to the uterus
questions.exp: Stage 1 is confined to the uterus, stage 2 spreads to pelvis and vagina, stage 3 to lung, and stage 4 to brain, liver or kidney. (Book p445)

questions.q: In the WHO risk scoring table, which pair falls in the HIGH-risk column?
opts: Age ≥ 40 years and antecedent full term pregnancy
questions.exp: High risk: age ≥40 yrs, full term antecedent, interval ≥12 months, hCG ≥10^5, size ≥5 cm, brain/liver sites, >8 mets, failed chemo. (Book p445)

questions.q: Fill up: WHO scoring assigns low risk for an interval between pregnancies of ______ and high risk for ______.
questions.exp: Interval <4 months scores low risk while ≥12 months scores high risk. (Book p445)

questions.q: Which hCG values mark the low- and high-risk ends of the WHO score?
questions.exp: Low risk hCG <10^3 IU; high risk ≥10^5 IU. (Book p445)

questions.q: Tumour size and number of metastases in the WHO score: low vs high risk.
opts: < 3 cm and < 4 mets vs ≥ 5 cm and > 8 mets
< 5 cm and < 8 mets vs ≥ 3 cm and > 4 mets
< 2 cm and < 2 mets vs ≥ 4 cm and > 6 mets
Size and mets are not scored
questions.exp: Low risk: <3 cm, <4 metastases; high risk: ≥5 cm, >8 metastases. (Book p445)

questions.q: Which metastatic sites score as high risk in WHO scoring?
questions.exp: Lung/vagina are low-risk sites; brain/liver are high-risk sites. (Book p445)

questions.q: Previous history of failed chemotherapy contributes to the WHO score as:
opts: Always high risk irrespective of history
questions.exp: Previous failed chemotherapy is (−) in the low-risk column and (+) in the high-risk column. (Book p445)

questions.q: Total WHO score interpretation: which cut-offs are used?
opts: ≤ 6 = low risk GTN; ≥ 7 = high risk GTN
questions.exp: Total score ≤6 is low risk GTN and ≥7 is high risk GTN. (Book p445)

questions.q: GTN is best described as:
questions.exp: GTN is chemosensitive, so chemotherapy is the backbone of management. (Book p445)

questions.q: Choose the correct treatment for stage 1 and stage 2–3 GTN with a WHO score < 6.
questions.exp: Stage 1 low risk and stage 2–3 with score <6 are treated with methotrexate. (Book p445)

questions.q: Stage 2–3 GTN with score ≥ 7, and all stage 4 disease, require:
questions.exp: Score ≥7 (stages 2–3) and stage 4 high-risk GTN receive multidrug chemotherapy. (Book p445)

questions.q: Fill up: In the WHO prognostic scoring system, a total score of ______ or more defines high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is treated with ______ chemotherapy.
questions.exp: A score of 6 or less is low risk and treated with single-agent chemotherapy; 7 or more is high risk and needs multi-agent EMA-CO. (Book p445)

questions.q: Which single drug is the DOC for low-risk GTN?
questions.exp: Methotrexate (MTX) is the DOC single-drug therapy. (Book p446)

questions.q: In multidose MTX therapy, the equally divided dose is given on which days, alternated with what?
questions.exp: Equally divided MTX doses on days 1, 3, 5, 7 are alternated with folic acid. (Book p446)

questions.q: After each MTX cycle, treatment is repeated until which endpoint, then followed up for how long?
opts: 3 consecutive normal β-hCG levels; follow-up 12 months
questions.exp: Cycles repeat till 3 consecutive normal β-hCG levels, with follow-up for 12 months. (Book p446)

questions.q: EMA-CO (Bagshaw regime) is also known as which multidrug therapy, and what does each letter-day pairing say?
opts: E etoposide D1, M MTX D2, A actinomycin D D3, C cyclophosphamide D4, O Oncovin D5
E etoposide D1, M MTX D1, A actinomycin D D1, C cisplatin D8, O Oncovin D8
E etoposide D4, M MTX D5, A actinomycin D D6, C cyclophosphamide D7, O Oncovin D8
E etoposide D2, M MTX D3, A actinomycin D D4, C cyclophosphamide D5, O Oncovin D6
questions.exp: As listed: etoposide D1, MTX D2, actinomycin D D3, cyclophosphamide D4, Oncovin D5. (Book p446)

questions.q: If GTN becomes resistant to EMA-CO, the regime switches to EMA-EP. What changes?
opts: Days 1–3 remain the same; etoposide on D4 and cisplatin on D5
All drugs stop and radiotherapy starts
questions.exp: In EMA-EP days 1, 2, 3 stay the same while etoposide is given on D4 and cisplatin on D5. (Book p446)

questions.q: Radiotherapy has a role in GTN for which metastatic site?
questions.exp: Radiotherapy is reserved for brain metastasis. (Book p446)

questions.q: Match the disease category with its treatment — 1) Low-risk GTN 2) High-risk GTN 3) Placental site trophoblastic tumour … A) Multi-agent EMA-CO chemotherapy B) Single-agent methotrexate or actinomycin D C) Hysterectomy, because it is relatively chemoresistant and secretes little hCG
questions.exp: Risk dictates intensity: single agent for low risk, EMA-CO for high risk, and surgery for the chemoresistant placental site tumour. (Book p446)

questions.q: How long is follow-up, and how long is pregnancy contraindicated, after multidrug GTN therapy?
opts: 12 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 12 months
6 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 6 months
12 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 24 months
24 months follow-up; pregnancy c/i for 6 months
questions.exp: Follow-up is for 12 months and pregnancy is contraindicated for 12 months. (Book p446)

questions.q: What is the management of PSTT/ETT?
questions.exp: PSTT/ETT is managed by hysterectomy followed by EMACO. (Book p446)

questions.q: Which tumour markers are listed for PSTT?
opts: Placental alkaline phosphatase and human placental lactogen
Beta-hCG and alpha-fetoprotein, both markedly elevated
CA-125 and inhibin, which closely track the tumour burden
Lactate dehydrogenase and calcitonin, which rise with metastases
questions.exp: Placental site trophoblastic tumour secretes placental alkaline phosphatase and human placental lactogen, with relatively little hCG. (Book p446)

questions.q: Which is NOT a listed indication of hysterectomy in GTD?
opts: Molar pregnancy with age ≥ 40 years + completed family
questions.exp: Indications are age ≥40 yrs with completed family, intractable hemorrhage during evacuation, PSTT/ETT, and stage I GTN with completed family. (Book p446)

questions.q: Stage I GTN in a woman with a completed family is managed by:
questions.exp: Stage I GTN with completed family: hysterectomy followed by multidose MTX. (Book p446)

questions.q: Match the histopathology: invasive mole vs choriocarcinoma vs PSTT.
opts: Invasive mole – edematous chorionic villi of syncytio- and cytotrophoblast; choriocarcinoma – no villi with syncytio- and cytotrophoblast; PSTT – no villi, intermediate trophoblast
Invasive mole – no villi; choriocarcinoma – edematous villi; PSTT – syncytiotrophoblast only
PSTT shows edematous villi; invasive mole shows intermediate trophoblast only
questions.exp: Invasive mole keeps edematous villi; choriocarcinoma has no villi-like structure with both trophoblasts; PSTT has no villi and intermediate trophoblast. (Book p446)

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the management of molar pregnancy is TRUE?
opts: Hysterectomy may suit a woman who has completed her family, but hCG follow-up is still needed because metastases can still appear
Hysterectomy removes all risk of malignant change, so no hCG follow-up is required
Prophylactic chemotherapy is given routinely after every molar evacuation
Combined oral contraceptives are contraindicated during follow-up because they raise hCG
questions.exp: Hysterectomy reduces but does not abolish the risk of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia; contraception during follow-up is encouraged, not banned. (Book p446)

units.title: signs & evacuation → follow-up & contraception
units.guide: Evacuate a mole by suction followed by sharp curettage while guarding against thyroid storm and embolism, then commit to a strict beta-hCG surveillance schedule and contraception plan. Focus for this checkpoint: Molar pregnancy: signs & evacuation, Molar pregnancy: follow-up & contraception.

units.title: Partial vs complete mole
units.guide: Separate partial from complete mole on genetics, p57 KIP2 staining, ultrasound, histology and malignant potential so the follow-up intensity is never misjudged. Focus for this checkpoint: Partial vs complete mole.

units.title: causes & clinical features → metastases
units.guide: Map each antecedent pregnancy to its possible neoplasia, read the beta-hCG plateau/rise criteria correctly and know where GTN metastasises and how it presents. Focus for this checkpoint: GTN: causes & clinical features, GTN: metastases.

units.title: FIGO staging & WHO scoring → risk-stratified management
units.sec: FIGO staging & WHO risk scoring · p445
units.guide: Stage GTN by FIGO site and score it with the WHO variables, then convert the total score into single-agent or multidrug therapy. Focus for this checkpoint: GTN: FIGO staging & WHO scoring, GTN: risk-stratified management.

units.title: chemotherapy regimens
units.guide: Recall the methotrexate day 1-3-5-7 folinic-acid alternating cycle and the EMA-CO day-by-day schedule, plus the EMA-EP switch for resistant disease. Focus for this checkpoint: GTN: chemotherapy regimens.

units.title: hysterectomy, follow-up & histopathology
units.guide: Know when hysterectomy replaces chemotherapy, how PSTT/ETT behave and how the three neoplasias differ under the microscope. Focus for this checkpoint: GTN: hysterectomy, follow-up & histopathology.
